claim: Heart of Glass (HEG1) is a transmembrane receptor essential for cardiovascular development.
source: Heart of Glass (HEG1), a transmembrane receptor, and Rasip1, an endothelial-specific Rap1-binding protein, are both essential for cardiovascular development.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known fact about HEG1, supported by citations in the introduction (Mably et al., 2003; Kleaveland et al., 2009).

claim: Rasip1 is an endothelial-specific Rap1-binding protein essential for cardiovascular development.
source: Heart of Glass (HEG1), a transmembrane receptor, and Rasip1, an endothelial-specific Rap1-binding protein, are both essential for cardiovascular development.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known fact about Rasip1, supported by citations in the introduction (Post et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: HEG1 binds directly to Rasip1.
source: Here we performed a proteomic screen for novel HEG1 interactors and report that HEG1 binds directly to Rasip1.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1B), immunoblotting (Figure 1C), and direct binding assays with purified proteins (Figure 5D).

claim: Rasip1 localizes to forming endothelial cell (EC) cell-cell junctions.
source: Rasip1 localizes to forming endothelial cell (EC) cell-cell junctions and silencing HEG1 prevents this localization.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing Rasip1 at VE-cadherin-positive cell-cell contacts (Figure 3A).

claim: Silencing HEG1 prevents Rasip1 localization to forming endothelial cell junctions.
source: Rasip1 localizes to forming endothelial cell (EC) cell-cell junctions and silencing HEG1 prevents this localization.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing loss of Rasip1 junctional localization in HEG1-silenced cells (Figure 3A, B).

claim: Mitochondria-targeted HEG1 relocalizes Rasip1 to mitochondria in cells.
source: Conversely, mitochondria-targeted HEG1 relocalizes Rasip1 to mitochondria in cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing endogenous Rasip1 recruited to mito-mCherry-HEG1 positive structures (Figure 1E).

claim: The Rasip1-binding site in HEG1 contains a 9 residue sequence (TDVYYSPTS).
source: The Rasip1-binding site in HEG1 contains a 9 residue sequence, deletion of which abrogates HEG1's ability to recruit Rasip1.
evidence: Demonstrated by deletion mapping studies showing that deletion of HEG1 aa 1327-1335 (TDVYYSPTS) prevents Rasip1 binding (Figure 4C, D, E).

claim: Deletion of the 9 residue sequence (TDVYYSPTS) in HEG1 abrogates HEG1's ability to recruit Rasip1.
source: The Rasip1-binding site in HEG1 contains a 9 residue sequence, deletion of which abrogates HEG1's ability to recruit Rasip1.
evidence: Demonstrated by binding assays and cellular localization studies showing loss of Rasip1 recruitment to HEG1(Δ1327-1335) (Figure 4C, D, E).

claim: HEG1 binds to a central region of Rasip1 containing the FHA domain.
source: HEG1 binds to a central region of Rasip1 and deletion of this domain eliminates Rasip1's ability to bind HEG1, to translocate to EC junctions, to inhibit ROCK activity, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by binding assays showing that Rasip1(266-550) containing the FHA domain is necessary and sufficient for HEG1 binding (Figure 5B, C, D).

claim: Deletion of the central FHA-containing domain of Rasip1 eliminates Rasip1's ability to bind HEG1.
source: HEG1 binds to a central region of Rasip1 and deletion of this domain eliminates Rasip1's ability to bind HEG1, to translocate to EC junctions, to inhibit ROCK activity, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by binding assays showing that Rasip1(Δ334-539) fails to bind HEG1 (Figure 5C).

claim: Deletion of the central FHA-containing domain of Rasip1 eliminates Rasip1's ability to translocate to EC junctions.
source: HEG1 binds to a central region of Rasip1 and deletion of this domain eliminates Rasip1's ability to bind HEG1, to translocate to EC junctions, to inhibit ROCK activity, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing that Rasip1(Δ334-539) fails to localize to cell-cell junctions (Figure 5E).

claim: Deletion of the central FHA-containing domain of Rasip1 eliminates Rasip1's ability to inhibit ROCK activity.
source: HEG1 binds to a central region of Rasip1 and deletion of this domain eliminates Rasip1's ability to bind HEG1, to translocate to EC junctions, to inhibit ROCK activity, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased MLC phosphorylation (a ROCK substrate) in cells expressing Rasip1(Δ334-539) (Figure 7A, B).

claim: Deletion of the central FHA-containing domain of Rasip1 eliminates Rasip1's ability to maintain EC junctional integrity.
source: HEG1 binds to a central region of Rasip1 and deletion of this domain eliminates Rasip1's ability to bind HEG1, to translocate to EC junctions, to inhibit ROCK activity, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased endothelial permeability in cells expressing Rasip1(Δ334-539) (Figure 7D).

claim: The binding of HEG1 to Rasip1 mediates Rap1-dependent recruitment of Rasip1 to EC cell-cell junctions.
source: These studies establish that the binding of HEG1 to Rasip1 mediates Rap1-dependent recruitment of Rasip1 to and stabilization of EC cell-cell junctions.
evidence: Demonstrated by the requirement of both HEG1 binding and Rap1 binding (via R182E mutant) for Rasip1 junctional localization (Figures 3, 8F, 9).

claim: The binding of HEG1 to Rasip1 mediates stabilization of EC cell-cell junctions.
source: These studies establish that the binding of HEG1 to Rasip1 mediates Rap1-dependent recruitment of Rasip1 to and stabilization of EC cell-cell junctions.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased permeability when HEG1-Rasip1 interaction is disrupted (Figure 7D).

claim: Rasip1 was identified as an HEG1 interactor in a proteomic screen using HUVEC lysates but not HeLa cell lysates.
source: This analysis identified a Rap1 effector, Rasip1, among the proteins isolated from endothelial cells but not from HeLa cells (Figure 1), a result consistent with the endothelial-specific expression of Rasip1 (Mitin et al., 2006; Mitin et al., 2004).
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis showing Rasip1 binding to HEG1 from HUVEC but not HeLa lysates (Figure 1B).

claim: Rasip1 expression is endothelial-specific.
source: This analysis identified a Rap1 effector, Rasip1, among the proteins isolated from endothelial cells but not from HeLa cells (Figure 1), a result consistent with the endothelial-specific expression of Rasip1 (Mitin et al., 2006; Mitin et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citations (Mitin et al., 2006; Mitin et al., 2004).

claim: KRIT1 was isolated from both HUVEC and HeLa cell lysates using HEG1 as bait.
source: In contrast KRIT1, and the known KRIT1 interactors CCM2 and ITGB1BP1 (ICAP1) (Zawistowski, 2005; Zawistowski, 2002) were isolated from both lysates.
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis (Figure 1B).

claim: CCM2 and ITGB1BP1 (ICAP1) are known KRIT1 interactors.
source: In contrast KRIT1, and the known KRIT1 interactors CCM2 and ITGB1BP1 (ICAP1) (Zawistowski, 2005; Zawistowski, 2002) were isolated from both lysates.
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citations (Zawistowski, 2005; Zawistowski, 2002).

claim: Deletion of the last 2 residues of the HEG1 tail (ΔYF) abolished binding of KRIT1, CCM2, and ITGB1BP1.
source: Moreover, deletion of the last 2 residues of the HEG1 tail abolished binding of KRIT1 as expected, and of the KRIT1-binding proteins CCM2 and ITGB1P1.
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry and immunoblotting showing loss of KRIT1, CCM2, and ITGB1BP1 binding to HEG1 ΔYF (Figure 1B, C).

claim: Rasip1 binding to HEG1 was not reduced by deletion of the YF motif.
source: In sharp contrast, Rasip1 binding was not reduced by the absence of the YF motif (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry and immunoblotting showing Rasip1 binding to both HEG1 WT and ΔYF (Figure 1B, C).

claim: Endogenous Rasip1 interacts with both the HEG1 cytoplasmic tail and HEG1 ΔYF.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed that endogenous Rasip1 interacts with both the HEG1 cytoplasmic tail and HEG1 ∆YF (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting of pull-down assays (Figure 1C).

claim: Rasip1 co-immunoprecipitated with full-length HEG1.
source: In addition, Rasip1 co-immunoprecipitated with full-length HEG1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1F).

claim: The HEG1-Rasip1 interaction does not require KRIT1 binding to HEG1.
source: Consistent with the mass spectrometry results, immunoblotting confirmed that Rasip1 bound to HEG1 ∆YF (Figure 1B,C), suggesting that the HEG1-Rasip1 interaction does not require KRIT1 binding to HEG1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rasip1 binds to HEG1 ΔYF, which cannot bind KRIT1, and confirmed by KRIT1 silencing experiments (Figure 2).

claim: Silencing KRIT1 expression did not affect binding of GFP-Rasip1 to the HEG1 cytoplasmic tail affinity matrix.
source: To further test the KRIT1-dependence of the HEG1-Rasip interaction, we silenced KRIT1 expression (Figure 2A,B; 70% reduction in expression was achieved) and found that it did not affect binding of GFP-Rasip1 to the HEG1 cytoplasmic tail affinity matrix (Figure 2A) or Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays in KRIT1-silenced cells (Figure 2A).

claim: Silencing KRIT1 expression did not affect Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1.
source: To further test the KRIT1-dependence of the HEG1-Rasip interaction, we silenced KRIT1 expression (Figure 2A,B; 70% reduction in expression was achieved) and found that it did not affect binding of GFP-Rasip1 to the HEG1 cytoplasmic tail affinity matrix (Figure 2A) or Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in KRIT1-silenced cells (Figure 2C).

claim: Rasip1 did not interact with the C-terminal 19 residues of HEG1, which are sufficient to bind KRIT1.
source: Conversely, Rasip1 did not interact with the C-terminal 19 residues of HEG1, which are sufficient to bind KRIT1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays showing no Rasip1 binding to HEG1 C19 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Rasip1 interacts with HEG1 independently of KRIT1.
source: Thus, we report that Rasip1 interacts with HEG1 independently of KRIT1.
evidence: Concluded from multiple lines of evidence including binding to HEG1 ΔYF, KRIT1 silencing experiments, and lack of binding to KRIT1-binding region (Figures 1, 2).

claim: Rasip1 redistributes from the endothelial cell cytoplasm to cell-cell junctions during the process of junction assembly.
source: Rasip1 redistributes from the endothelial cell cytoplasm to cell-cell junctions during the process of junction assembly (Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citation (Wilson et al., 2013) and demonstrated in the current study (Figure 3A).

claim: HEG1 is found in endothelial cell-cell junctions.
source: Because HEG1 is found in these junctions (Kleaveland et al., 2009), we hypothesized that the HEG1-Rasip1 interaction might mediate Rasip1 recruitment.
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citation (Kleaveland et al., 2009).

claim: During junction assembly induced by calcium switch and Rap1 activation, Rasip1 was recruited to VE-cadherin-positive cell-cell contacts.
source: As expected, during junction assembly, Rasip1 was recruited to VE-cadherin-positive cell-cell contacts (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing Rasip1 colocalization with VE-cadherin at junctions (Figure 3A).

claim: When HEG1 was silenced, Rasip1 recruitment to cell-cell contacts was prevented.
source: In sharp contrast, when HEG1 was silenced (Figure 3C) Rasip1 recruitment to cell-cell contacts was prevented (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing loss of Rasip1 junctional localization in HEG1-silenced cells (Figure 3A, B).

claim: Silencing HEG1 expression with a second shRNA prevented Rasip1 recruitment to EC contacts.
source: To exclude off-target effects, silencing HEG1 expression with a second shRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or an siRNA specific for HEG1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) also prevented Rasip1 recruitment to EC contacts.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy using independent HEG1 knockdown reagents (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: Loss of HEG1-KRIT1 interaction increases Rho-Kinase (ROCK) activity.
source: Previous studies have shown that loss of HEG1-KRIT1 interaction increases Rho-Kinase (ROCK) activity (Gingras et al., 2012), however, a ROCK inhibitor, H-1152, did not restore Rasip1 recruitment in HEG1-silenced EC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citation (Gingras et al., 2012).

claim: A ROCK inhibitor (H-1152) did not restore Rasip1 recruitment in HEG1-silenced EC.
source: Previous studies have shown that loss of HEG1-KRIT1 interaction increases Rho-Kinase (ROCK) activity (Gingras et al., 2012), however, a ROCK inhibitor, H-1152, did not restore Rasip1 recruitment in HEG1-silenced EC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing no rescue of Rasip1 junctional localization with ROCK inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).

claim: Silencing of KRIT1 did not prevent Rasip1 recruitment to cell-cell contacts during junction formation.
source: Moreover, silencing of KRIT1 (Figure 2B) did not prevent Rasip1 recruitment to cell-cell contacts during junction formation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing Rasip1 junctional localization in KRIT1-silenced cells (Figure 3D).

claim: HEG1 mediates Rasip1 recruitment to forming EC junctions.
source: Thus, HEG1 mediates Rasip1 recruitment to forming EC junctions.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that HEG1 silencing prevents Rasip1 junctional localization while KRIT1 silencing does not (Figures 3, 2).

claim: Rasip1 regulates β1 integrin activation.
source: Rasip1 regulates β1 integrin activation (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citation (Xu et al., 2011) and confirmed in the current study (Figure 6A).

claim: Silencing Rasip1 expression in HUVEC decreased 9EG7 binding (activated β1 integrin).
source: As expected, silencing Rasip1 expression in HUVEC decreased 9EG7 binding.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry measuring 9EG7 antibody binding (Figure 6A).

claim: Silencing HEG1 expression did not affect levels of activated β1 integrin.
source: In contrast, silencing HEG1 expression did not affect levels of activated β1 integrin (Figure 6A) suggesting that the effect of Rasip1 on β1 integrin activation is independent of HEG1.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry showing no change in 9EG7 binding in HEG1-silenced cells (Figure 6A).

claim: The effect of Rasip1 on β1 integrin activation is independent of HEG1.
source: In contrast, silencing HEG1 expression did not affect levels of activated β1 integrin (Figure 6A) suggesting that the effect of Rasip1 on β1 integrin activation is independent of HEG1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HEG1 silencing does not affect β1 integrin activation while Rasip1 silencing does (Figure 6A).

claim: Rasip1 mediates Rap1 inhibition of RhoA activity and of the RhoA effector Rho kinase (ROCK).
source: Previous studies show that Rasip1 mediates Rap1 inhibition of RhoA activity and of the RhoA effector Rho kinase (ROCK).
evidence: Stated as known fact from previous studies, supported by citations in the introduction (Xu et al., 2011; Post et al., 2013).

claim: Silencing Rasip1 expression in endothelial cells can increase phosphorylation of myosin light chain 2 (MLC), a ROCK substrate.
source: As a result, silencing Rasip1 expression in endothelial cells can increase phosphorylation of a ROCK substrate, myosin light chain 2 (MLC) (Xu et al., 2011), resulting in increased actin stress fibers and reduced cortical actin (Post et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citations (Xu et al., 2011; Post et al., 2013) and confirmed in the current study (Figure 6C, 7A).

claim: Silencing HEG1 expression in HUVEC increased phosphorylation of MLC and formation of stress fibers.
source: Similar to silencing Rasip1, silencing HEG1 expression in HUVEC by siRNA or shRNA increased phosphorylation of MLC and formation of stress fibers indicating increased ROCK signaling (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing increased pMLC and stress fibers in HEG1-silenced cells (Figure 6B, C).

claim: Silencing HEG1 expression increased MLC phosphorylation and formation of actin stress fibers, which was rescued by expressing shRNA-resistant murine HEG1.
source: Silencing HEG1 expression in HUVEC increased MLC phosphorylation and formation of actin stress fibers, which was rescued by expressing shRNA-resistant murine HEG1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing rescue of pMLC and stress fiber phenotype with wild-type mHEG1 expression (Figure 6D).

claim: Expression of Rasip1-binding deficient murine HEG1(∆1283-1291) failed to rescue the increase in MLC phosphorylation and actin stress fiber formation.
source: However, expression of Rasip1-binding deficient murine HEG1(∆1283-1291) (corresponding to aa 1327-1335 in human HEG1) failed to rescue the increase in MLC phosphorylation and actin stress fiber formation (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing no rescue with mHEG1(Δ1283-1291) expression (Figure 6D).

claim: Silencing expression of Rasip1 increased MLC phosphorylation by ~40%.
source: Conversely, silencing expression of Rasip1 increased MLC phosphorylation by ~40% (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 7A, B).

claim: Expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type Rasip1 rescued increased MLC phosphorylation caused by Rasip1 silencing.
source: Expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type Rasip1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) rescued increased MLC phosphorylation (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 7A, B).

claim: HEG1-binding deficient Rasip1(∆334-539) failed to rescue increased MLC phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, HEG1-binding deficient Rasip1(∆334-539) failed to rescue increased MLC phosphorylation (Figure 7A,B)
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 7A, B).

claim: Expression of Rasip1(∆334-539) induced increased MLC phosphorylation even in the absence of Rasip1 silencing.
source: Moreover, expression of Rasip1(∆334-539) induced increased MLC phosphorylation even in the absence of Rasip1 silencing, indicating that it could act in a dominant negative manner (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing increased pMLC in cells expressing Rasip1(Δ334-539) without Rasip1 knockdown (Figure 7C).

claim: Rasip1(∆334-539) can act in a dominant negative manner.
source: Moreover, expression of Rasip1(∆334-539) induced increased MLC phosphorylation even in the absence of Rasip1 silencing, indicating that it could act in a dominant negative manner (Figure 7C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rasip1(Δ334-539) expression increases pMLC without Rasip1 knockdown (Figure 7C).

claim: The interaction between Rasip1 and HEG1 is important for regulation of RhoA/ROCK signaling and the actin cytoskeleton in endothelial cells.
source: These data show that the interaction between Rasip1 and HEG1 is important for regulation of RhoA/ROCK signaling and the actin cytoskeleton in endothelial cells.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that disruption of HEG1-Rasip1 interaction increases ROCK activity and stress fibers (Figures 6, 7).

claim: Deletion of 9 amino acids in HEG1 (aa 1327-1335; TDVYYSPTS) prevented binding of Rasip1 to HEG1 in vitro.
source: Deletion of 9 amino acids in HEG1 (aa 1327-1335; TDVYYSPTS) prevented binding of Rasip1 to HEG1 in vitro (Figure 4C), Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 4D), and co-immunoprecipitation of Rasip1 with murine HEG1(∆1283-1291) (corresponding to aa 1327-1335 in human HEG1; Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays (Figure 4C).

claim: Deletion of HEG1 aa 1327-1335 prevented Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1.
source: Deletion of 9 amino acids in HEG1 (aa 1327-1335; TDVYYSPTS) prevented binding of Rasip1 to HEG1 in vitro (Figure 4C), Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 4D), and co-immunoprecipitation of Rasip1 with murine HEG1(∆1283-1291) (corresponding to aa 1327-1335 in human HEG1; Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 4D).

claim: Deletion of HEG1 aa 1327-1335 prevented co-immunoprecipitation of Rasip1 with murine HEG1.
source: Deletion of 9 amino acids in HEG1 (aa 1327-1335; TDVYYSPTS) prevented binding of Rasip1 to HEG1 in vitro (Figure 4C), Rasip1 recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 4D), and co-immunoprecipitation of Rasip1 with murine HEG1(∆1283-1291) (corresponding to aa 1327-1335 in human HEG1; Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4E).

claim: A 22-mer encompassing HEG1 region 1318-1339, which lacked KRIT1 binding, was sufficient to interact with Rasip1.
source: Furthermore, a 22-mer encompassing this region (HEG1 1318-1339), which lacked KRIT1 binding, was sufficient to interact with Rasip1 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays showing Rasip1 binding to HEG1(1318-1339) (Figure 4B, C).

claim: The Rasip1 binding site in HEG1 was mapped to a 9 residue peptide (TDVYYSPTS).
source: Thus, we mapped the Rasip1 binding site in HEG1 to a 9 residue peptide and show that deletion of this sequence blocks the capacity of HEG1 to bind to and to recruit Rasip1.
evidence: Concluded from deletion mapping studies (Figure 4).

claim: Rasip1(266-550), containing the FHA domain, was sufficient for binding to HEG1.
source: Rasip1(266-550), containing the FHA domain, was sufficient for binding to HEG1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays showing binding of Rasip1(266-550) to HEG1 (Figure 5B).

claim: Deletion of the FHA-containing region in Rasip1(∆334-539) disrupted HEG1 binding.
source: Next, we tested whether this region is necessary for binding to HEG1. Deletion of this region in Rasip1(∆334-539) (Figure 5A) disrupted HEG1 binding (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays showing loss of HEG1 binding to Rasip1(Δ334-539) (Figure 5C).

claim: The region of Rasip1 encompassing the FHA domain is both necessary and sufficient to bind to HEG1.
source: Thus, the region of Rasip1 encompassing the FHA domain is both necessary and sufficient to bind to HEG1.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that Rasip1(266-550) is sufficient and deletion of this region abolishes binding (Figure 5B, C).

claim: The interaction of HEG1 and the FHA domain of Rasip1 was direct.
source: Furthermore, the interaction of HEG1 and the FHA domain was direct because purified Rasip1(266-550) bound to both HEG1, HEG1 ∆YF, or HEG1(1318-1339) peptide affinity matrices (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by direct binding assays using purified recombinant proteins (Figure 5D).

claim: HEG1 binds directly to the FHA domain of Rasip1 via a 9 amino acid (TDVYYSPTS) region of HEG1.
source: Thus, HEG1 binds directly to the FHA domain of Rasip1 via a 9 amino acid (TDVYYSPTS) region of HEG1.
evidence: Concluded from mapping studies and direct binding assays (Figures 4, 5).

claim: Deletion of the HEG1-binding central domain of Rasip1 abolished recruitment of Rasip1(∆334-539) to endothelial cell-cell junctions.
source: Deletion of the HEG1-binding central domain of Rasip1 abolished recruitment of Rasip1(∆334-539) to these junctions (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing no junctional localization of Rasip1(Δ334-539) (Figure 5E).

claim: Rasip1 is known to associate with cytoplasmic vesicles.
source: Rasip1 is known to associate with cytoplasmic vesicles (Xu et al., 2011; Mitin et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citations (Xu et al., 2011; Mitin et al., 2004).

claim: Rasip1(∆334-539) accumulated on cytoplasmic vesicles, which often appeared to concentrate near cell-cell junctions.
source: Remarkably, Rasip1(∆334-539) accumulated on cytoplasmic vesicles, which often appeared to concentrate near cell-cell junctions; however, in contrast to the full length protein, Rasip1(∆334-539) never incorporated into the junctions.
evidence: Observed by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 5E).

claim: Rasip1(∆334-539) never incorporated into cell-cell junctions.
source: Remarkably, Rasip1(∆334-539) accumulated on cytoplasmic vesicles, which often appeared to concentrate near cell-cell junctions; however, in contrast to the full length protein, Rasip1(∆334-539) never incorporated into the junctions.
evidence: Observed by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 5E).

claim: The region of Rasip1 that mediates its physical interaction with HEG1 is required for Rasip1 junctional localization.
source: Thus, the region of Rasip1 that mediates its physical interaction with HEG1 is required for Rasip1 junctional localization.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that Rasip1(Δ334-539), which cannot bind HEG1, fails to localize to junctions (Figure 5E).

claim: Silencing of Rasip1 increases endothelial permeability.
source: Silencing of Rasip1 increases endothelial permeability (Post et al., 2013; Post et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citations (Post et al., 2013; Post et al., 2015) and confirmed in the current study (Figure 7D).

claim: Silencing Rasip1 increased endothelial permeability, and this was rescued by expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type Rasip1.
source: As expected, silencing Rasip1 increased endothelial permeability, and this was rescued by expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type (WT) Rasip1 (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by transwell permeability assays (Figure 7D).

claim: HEG1-binding deficient Rasip1(∆334-539) failed to reverse increased endothelial cell permeability.
source: In contrast, HEG1-binding deficient Rasip1(∆334-539) failed to reverse increased endothelial cell permeability (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by transwell permeability assays (Figure 7D).

claim: Deletion of the HEG1 binding domain of Rasip1 abolishes the capacity of Rasip1 to translocate to cell-cell contacts, to inhibit ROCK, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
source: Thus, deletion of the HEG1 binding domain of Rasip1 abolishes the capacity of Rasip1 to translocate to cell-cell contacts, to inhibit ROCK, and to maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that Rasip1(Δ334-539) fails in junctional localization, ROCK inhibition, and permeability rescue (Figures 5E, 7).

claim: Rap1 binding regulates the capacity of Rasip1 to target to HEG1-containing junctions.
source: We found that Rasip1 and KRIT1 bound to HEG1 at distinct binding sites. Rap1 binding regulates the capacity of both proteins to target to HEG1-containing junctions, inhibit ROCK activity, and maintain junctional integrity (Figure 10).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with Rap1-binding deficient Rasip1(R182E) (Figures 8F, 9).

claim: Rap1 binding regulates the capacity of Rasip1 to inhibit ROCK activity.
source: We found that Rasip1 and KRIT1 bound to HEG1 at distinct binding sites. Rap1 binding regulates the capacity of both proteins to target to HEG1-containing junctions, inhibit ROCK activity, and maintain junctional integrity (Figure 10).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that Rap1-binding deficient Rasip1(R182E) fails to inhibit ROCK (Figure 9A, B).

claim: Rap1 binding regulates the capacity of Rasip1 to maintain junctional integrity.
source: We found that Rasip1 and KRIT1 bound to HEG1 at distinct binding sites. Rap1 binding regulates the capacity of both proteins to target to HEG1-containing junctions, inhibit ROCK activity, and maintain junctional integrity (Figure 10).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that Rap1-binding deficient Rasip1(R182E) fails to rescue permeability (Figure 9C).

claim: The Rasip1 murine null phenotype is lethal by day E9.5 with much more profound vascular collapse than is seen in the Heg1 null.
source: Importantly, the Rasip1 murine null phenotype is lethal by day E9.5 with much more profound vascular collapse (Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013) than is seen in the Heg1 null (Kleaveland et al., 2009) suggesting that Rasip1 has functions that do not depend on HEG1 binding or recruitment to EC junctions.
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citations (Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013; Kleaveland et al., 2009).

claim: Rasip1 has functions that do not depend on HEG1 binding or recruitment to EC junctions.
source: Importantly, the Rasip1 murine null phenotype is lethal by day E9.5 with much more profound vascular collapse (Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013) than is seen in the Heg1 null (Kleaveland et al., 2009) suggesting that Rasip1 has functions that do not depend on HEG1 binding or recruitment to EC junctions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rasip1 null phenotype is more severe than HEG1 null phenotype.

claim: Rasip1 null mice exhibit profound detachment of EC from their basement membranes.
source: One compelling possibility is that Rasip1 null mice exhibit profound detachment of EC from their basement membranes (Xu et al., 2011), perhaps due to inhibition of integrin activation.
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citation (Xu et al., 2011).

claim: The Rap1-regulated interaction of HEG1 with Rasip1 localizes Rasip1 to endothelial cell junctions and stabilizes them.
source: Thus, the Rap1-regulated interaction of HEG1 with Rasip1 localizes Rasip1 to those junctions and stabilizes them.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that HEG1 binding and Rap1 binding are required for Rasip1 junctional localization and function (Figures 3, 7, 8, 9).

claim: Rap1 regulated association of KRIT1 with a second site in HEG1 also contributes to vascular development and integrity.
source: Remarkably, Rap1 regulated association of KRIT1 with a second site in HEG1 also contributes to vascular development and integrity.
evidence: Stated as known fact from previous studies, supported by citations in the introduction (Gingras et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2011; Glading et al., 2007; Béraud-Dufour et al., 2007; Gingras et al., 2012).

claim: HEG1 serves as physical nexus of Rap effectors that control both RhoA/ROCK signaling and vascular development.
source: Thus, HEG1 serves as physical nexus of Rap effectors that control both RhoA/ROCK signaling and vascular development.
evidence: Concluded from the finding that HEG1 binds both Rasip1 and KRIT1, both of which are Rap1 effectors that regulate ROCK signaling.

claim: The 111 amino acid HEG1 cytoplasmic domain is highly conserved (e.g. 76% identity between human and zebrafish).
source: The 111 amino acid HEG1 cytoplasmic domain is highly conserved (e.g. 76% identity between human and zebrafish) whereas KRIT1 binding requires only the C-terminal 10% of HEG1 tail (Gingras et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as a fact about HEG1 sequence conservation.

claim: KRIT1 binding requires only the C-terminal 10% of HEG1 tail.
source: The 111 amino acid HEG1 cytoplasmic domain is highly conserved (e.g. 76% identity between human and zebrafish) whereas KRIT1 binding requires only the C-terminal 10% of HEG1 tail (Gingras et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as known fact supported by citation (Gingras et al., 2012).

claim: Precisely regulated cell-cell adhesion is crucial for the development and functioning of multicellular organisms.
source: Precisely regulated cell-cell adhesion is crucial for the development and functioning of multicellular organisms (Nelson, 2008).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Nelson, 2008).

claim: In vascular endothelial cells, cell-cell contacts formed by adherens and tight junctions control vascular patterning and provide a barrier to the passage of water and solutes.
source: In vascular endothelial cells (EC), cell-cell contacts formed by adherens and tight junctions (Bazzoni, 2004), control vascular patterning and provide a barrier to the passage of water and solutes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Bazzoni, 2004).

claim: Weakening of the endothelial barrier contributes to diseases such as sepsis, atherosclerosis, and multiple sclerosis.
source: Weakening of this endothelial barrier contributes to diseases such as sepsis, atherosclerosis, and multiple sclerosis (Bazzoni, 2004; Dejana et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Bazzoni, 2004; Dejana et al., 2009).

claim: The actin cytoskeleton and its regulatory Rho GTPases have profound roles in the assembly and disassembly of cell-cell contacts.
source: The actin cytoskeleton (Mège et al., 2006) and its regulatory Rho GTPases have profound roles in the assembly and disassembly of cell-cell contacts (Beckers et al., 2010; Yamada and Nelson, 2007).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Mège et al., 2006; Beckers et al., 2010; Yamada and Nelson, 2007).

claim: Rap1, a small GTPase, regulates epithelial and EC cell-cell adhesion.
source: Rap1, a small GTPase, regulates epithelial and EC cell-cell adhesion (Pannekoek et al., 2014; Kooistra et al., 2007; Knox, 2002).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Pannekoek et al., 2014; Kooistra et al., 2007; Knox, 2002).

claim: In EC, binding of activated Rap1 to KRIT1 targets KRIT1 to cell-cell contacts.
source: In EC, binding of activated Rap1 to KRIT1 (Gingras et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012), a scaffold that regulates RhoA signaling (Whitehead et al., 2009; Stockton et al., 2010), targets KRIT1 to cell-cell contacts (Liu et al., 2011; Glading et al., 2007; Béraud-Dufour et al., 2007) where it directly interacts with Heart of Glass (HEG1) (Gingras et al., 2012), a transmembrane receptor essential for cardiovascular development (Mably et al., 2003; Kleaveland et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Gingras et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2011; Glading et al., 2007; Béraud-Dufour et al., 2007).

claim: KRIT1 is a scaffold that regulates RhoA signaling.
source: In EC, binding of activated Rap1 to KRIT1 (Gingras et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012), a scaffold that regulates RhoA signaling (Whitehead et al., 2009; Stockton et al., 2010), targets KRIT1 to cell-cell contacts (Liu et al., 2011; Glading et al., 2007; Béraud-Dufour et al., 2007) where it directly interacts with Heart of Glass (HEG1) (Gingras et al., 2012), a transmembrane receptor essential for cardiovascular development (Mably et al., 2003; Kleaveland et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Whitehead et al., 2009; Stockton et al., 2010).

claim: KRIT1 directly interacts with Heart of Glass (HEG1).
source: In EC, binding of activated Rap1 to KRIT1 (Gingras et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012), a scaffold that regulates RhoA signaling (Whitehead et al., 2009; Stockton et al., 2010), targets KRIT1 to cell-cell contacts (Liu et al., 2011; Glading et al., 2007; Béraud-Dufour et al., 2007) where it directly interacts with Heart of Glass (HEG1) (Gingras et al., 2012), a transmembrane receptor essential for cardiovascular development (Mably et al., 2003; Kleaveland et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Gingras et al., 2012).

claim: Rasip1 is a Rap1 binding protein essential for vascular integrity and development.
source: Here, we report an unbiased proteomic screen for HEG1-binding endothelial-specific proteins that revealed that Rasip1, a second Rap1 binding protein essential for vascular integrity and development (Post et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013), directly interacts with the HEG1 cytoplasmic domain independent of KRIT1.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Post et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: Rasip1 directly interacts with the HEG1 cytoplasmic domain independent of KRIT1.
source: Here, we report an unbiased proteomic screen for HEG1-binding endothelial-specific proteins that revealed that Rasip1, a second Rap1 binding protein essential for vascular integrity and development (Post et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2013), directly interacts with the HEG1 cytoplasmic domain independent of KRIT1.
evidence: Demonstrated by proteomic screen, binding assays, and KRIT1 silencing experiments (Figures 1, 2).

claim: A structure-based Rasip1 RA-domain mutant (R182E) failed to bind to Rap1.
source: We designed a structure-based Rasip1 RA-domain mutant (R182E) that failed to bind to Rap1 and did not associate with HEG1 in cells or maintain EC barrier integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography showing loss of Rap1 binding (Figure 8D).

claim: Rasip1 RA-domain mutant (R182E) did not associate with HEG1 in cells.
source: We designed a structure-based Rasip1 RA-domain mutant (R182E) that failed to bind to Rap1 and did not associate with HEG1 in cells or maintain EC barrier integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing no recruitment to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 8F).

claim: Rasip1 RA-domain mutant (R182E) did not maintain EC barrier integrity.
source: We designed a structure-based Rasip1 RA-domain mutant (R182E) that failed to bind to Rap1 and did not associate with HEG1 in cells or maintain EC barrier integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by permeability assays showing failure to rescue increased permeability (Figure 9C).

claim: HEG1 interacts with two different Rap1 effectors (Rasip1 and KRIT1) important in EC.
source: These studies reveal that HEG1 interacts with two different Rap1 effectors important in EC, indicating that this transmembrane receptor serves as a physical nexus for Rap1 signaling in vascular integrity and development.
evidence: Demonstrated by the current study showing HEG1-Rasip1 interaction and previous studies showing HEG1-KRIT1 interaction.

claim: HEG1 serves as a physical nexus for Rap1 signaling in vascular integrity and development.
source: These studies reveal that HEG1 interacts with two different Rap1 effectors important in EC, indicating that this transmembrane receptor serves as a physical nexus for Rap1 signaling in vascular integrity and development.
evidence: Concluded from the finding that HEG1 binds both Rasip1 and KRIT1, both Rap1 effectors.

claim: The Rasip1 RA domain sequence is similar to those found in RalGDS, Afadin6, and Radil.
source: Comparison of the Rasip1 RA domain sequence showed that it was similar to those found in RalGDS, Afadin6, and Radil.
evidence: Stated based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Sequence alignment of Rasip1 RA domain with Radil shows a highly conserved sequence (31% identical).
source: Sequence alignment of Rasip1 RA domain with Radil shows a highly conserved sequence (31% identical, Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment (Figure 8A).

claim: A preliminary homology model of the Rasip1 RA domain closely resembles the structure of Radil RA domain.
source: A preliminary homology model of the Rasip1 RA domain closely resembles the structure of Radil RA domain (PDB ID 3EC8) (backbone rmsd 1.02Å for 126 a.a., Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by homology modeling (Figure 8B).

claim: The Radil crystal structure shows a dimer that is stabilized by an extensive interface burying 30% (2,324 Å2) of the total surface area of each monomer.
source: The Radil crystal structure shows a dimer that is stabilized by an extensive interface burying 30% (2,324 Å2) of the total surface area of each monomer (Figure 8B, highlighted in blue).
evidence: Stated based on analysis of the Radil crystal structure (PDB 3EC8).

claim: The dimer interface is conserved in Rasip1.
source: Analysis of our model shows that the dimer interface is conserved in Rasip1 (Figure 8B, magenta and yellow), suggesting that it could also form a dimer similar to Radil RA domain and therefore could bind two Rap1 molecules per dimer (Figure 8C).
evidence: Demonstrated by homology modeling and sequence analysis (Figure 8B).

claim: Rasip1 RA domain could form a dimer similar to Radil RA domain.
source: Analysis of our model shows that the dimer interface is conserved in Rasip1 (Figure 8B, magenta and yellow), suggesting that it could also form a dimer similar to Radil RA domain and therefore could bind two Rap1 molecules per dimer (Figure 8C).
evidence: Inferred from conservation of dimer interface and confirmed by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 8D).

claim: Purified recombinant Rasip1 RA domain (residues 134-285) forms a dimer in solution.
source: Indeed, purified recombinant Rasip1 RA domain (residues 134-285) eluted earlier than expected from its monomer mass (16.3kDa) in size exclusion chromatography (SEC), suggesting that it forms a dimer (~35kDa) in solution (Figure 8D; green).
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 8D).

claim: The purified Rasip1 RA domain bound activated Rap1B.
source: The purified Rasip1 RA domain bound activated Rap1B (Figure 8D; red) and Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) measured a kd = 0.77 ± 0.09 μM for the interaction (Figure 8E).
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography and isothermal titration calorimetry (Figure 8D, E).

claim: The binding affinity between Rasip1 RA domain and Rap1B is kd = 0.77 ± 0.09 μM.
source: The purified Rasip1 RA domain bound activated Rap1B (Figure 8D; red) and Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) measured a kd = 0.77 ± 0.09 μM for the interaction (Figure 8E).
evidence: Measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (Figure 8E).

claim: Rasip1(R182E) exhibited a markedly reduced affinity for Rap1.
source: SEC revealed that Rasip1(R182E) exhibited a markedly reduced affinity for Rap1 (Figure 8D; black).
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography showing no complex formation (Figure 8D).

claim: The Rasip1(R182E) mutant was well folded.
source: Moreover, SEC showed that the Rasip1(R182E) mutant was well folded and exhibited the same elution pattern in SEC as the wild-type protein.
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography showing similar elution pattern to wild-type (Figure 8D).

claim: Rasip1 RA domain (R182E) remains well folded as a multimer but binds Rap1 with drastically reduced affinity.
source: Thus, we conclude that Rasip1 RA domain (R182E) remains well folded as a multimer but binds Rap1 with drastically reduced affinity.
evidence: Concluded from size exclusion chromatography data (Figure 8D).

claim: Rasip1(R182E) was not targeted to mito-mCherry-HEG1.
source: We examined the capacity of Rasip1(R182E) to localize with HEG1 in cells and found that this mutant was not targeted to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 8F).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 8F).

claim: In living cells, Rasip1 recruitment to HEG1 is lost when a point mutant disrupts its capacity to bind Rap1.
source: Thus, in living cells, Rasip1 recruitment to HEG1 is lost when a point mutant disrupts its capacity to bind Rap1.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that Rasip1(R182E) does not localize to mito-mCherry-HEG1 (Figure 8F).

claim: Rasip1(R182E) failed to rescue the effect of silencing of Rasip1 on increased MLC phosphorylation.
source: Rasip1(R182E) also failed to rescue the effect of silencing of Rasip1 on increased MLC phosphorylation or endothelial permeability (Figure 9A–C) although it was well expressed (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 9A, B).

claim: Rasip1(R182E) failed to rescue the effect of silencing of Rasip1 on endothelial permeability.
source: Rasip1(R182E) also failed to rescue the effect of silencing of Rasip1 on increased MLC phosphorylation or endothelial permeability (Figure 9A–C) although it was well expressed (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated by permeability assays (Figure 9C).

claim: Rasip1(R182E) is well expressed and folded, binds to activated Rap1 with much reduced affinity and loses the capacity to interact with HEG1 in living cells, and to inhibit ROCK and maintain EC junctional integrity.
source: Thus, Rasip1(R182E) is well expressed and folded, binds to activated Rap1 with much reduced affinity and loses the capacity to interact with HEG1 in living cells, and to inhibit ROCK and maintain EC junctional integrity.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments characterizing Rasip1(R182E) (Figures 8, 9).

claim: Silencing HEG1 did not affect the interaction between Rasip1 and Radil.
source: As expected, Radil and ARHGAP29 co-immunoprecipitated with Rasip1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B). Silencing HEG1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C; 75% reduction in mRNA expression was achieved) did not affect the interaction between Rasip1 and Radil or ARHGAP29 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Silencing HEG1 did not affect the interaction between Rasip1 and ARHGAP29.
source: As expected, Radil and ARHGAP29 co-immunoprecipitated with Rasip1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B). Silencing HEG1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C; 75% reduction in mRNA expression was achieved) did not affect the interaction between Rasip1 and Radil or ARHGAP29 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: Rasip1 interacted with constitutively active Rap1-V12.
source: Next we tested whether HEG1 could regulate the interaction between Rasip1 and Rap1. Rasip1 interacted with constitutively active Rap1-V12; the interaction was not affected by silencing HEG1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: The interaction between Rasip1 and Rap1-V12 was not affected by silencing HEG1 expression.
source: Next we tested whether HEG1 could regulate the interaction between Rasip1 and Rap1. Rasip1 interacted with constitutively active Rap1-V12; the interaction was not affected by silencing HEG1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEG1-silenced cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: Addition of purified HEG1 cytoplasmic tail peptide (5 µM) did not alter the interaction between Rap1-V12 and Rasip1.
source: Similarly, addition of purified HEG1 cytoplasmic tail peptide (5 µM) did not alter the interaction between Rap1-V12 and Rasip1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with added HEG1 peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: HEG1 is required for Rasip1 translocation to cell-cell contacts.
source: These data suggest that HEG1 is required for Rasip1 translocation to cell-cell contacts; however, formation of a Rasip1-Rap1 or Rasip1-Radil-ARHGAP29 complex is not dependent on the presence of HEG1.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that HEG1 silencing prevents Rasip1 junctional localization (Figure 3).

claim: Formation of a Rasip1-Rap1 complex is not dependent on the presence of HEG1.
source: These data suggest that HEG1 is required for Rasip1 translocation to cell-cell contacts; however, formation of a Rasip1-Rap1 or Rasip1-Radil-ARHGAP29 complex is not dependent on the presence of HEG1.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that HEG1 silencing does not affect Rasip1-Rap1 interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: Formation of a Rasip1-Radil-ARHGAP29 complex is not dependent on the presence of HEG1.
source: These data suggest that HEG1 is required for Rasip1 translocation to cell-cell contacts; however, formation of a Rasip1-Rap1 or Rasip1-Radil-ARHGAP29 complex is not dependent on the presence of HEG1.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that HEG1 silencing does not affect Rasip1-Radil or Rasip1-ARHGAP29 interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).

claim: At cell-cell contacts, Rasip1, in conjunction with the Rap1 effector Radil, suppresses RhoA/ROCK signaling via the RhoA RhoGAP ARHGAP29.
source: At cell-cell contacts, Rasip1, in conjunction with the Rap1 effector Radil, suppresses RhoA/ROCK signaling via the RhoA RhoGAP ARHGAP29 (Post et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011; Post et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Post et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011; Post et al., 2015).

claim: Rasip1(∆334-539) transport to the cell periphery is intact.
source: We noted (Figure 5E) that Rasip1(∆334-539) appears to accumulate on vesicles, suggesting that Rasip1(∆334-539) transport to the cell periphery is intact but that incorporation into cell-cell contacts depends on HEG1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rasip1(Δ334-539) accumulates on vesicles near junctions but does not incorporate into them (Figure 5E).

claim: Incorporation of Rasip1 into cell-cell contacts depends on HEG1.
source: We noted (Figure 5E) that Rasip1(∆334-539) appears to accumulate on vesicles, suggesting that Rasip1(∆334-539) transport to the cell periphery is intact but that incorporation into cell-cell contacts depends on HEG1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rasip1(Δ334-539), which cannot bind HEG1, fails to incorporate into junctions (Figure 5E).

claim: The junctional localization of Rasip1 is important for regulation of RhoA/ROCK and vascular permeability.
source: Our finding that HEG1-binding defective Rasip1(∆334-539), which did not reach EC junctions, failed to rescue both increased phospho-myosin and vascular permeability caused by Rasip1 silencing, supports the idea (Post et al., 2015) that the junctional localization of Rasip1 is important for regulation of RhoA/ROCK and vascular permeability.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that Rasip1(Δ334-539), which fails to localize to junctions, also fails to rescue ROCK activity and permeability (Figures 5E, 7).
